physics-001.question: what and why
physics-001.line: A heavier object is pulled harder by gravity, but it is also harder to get moving. These two effects cancel exactly.

physics-001.question: how
physics-001.line: On Earth, air pushes back much more on a feather than on a hammer, which is why the feather falls slowly.

physics-001.question: when
physics-001.line: Take the air away and they fall together.

physics-001.question: where, when and who
physics-001.line: Apollo 15 (1971): Commander David Scott dropped a geologic hammer and a feather together on the Moon, where there is almost no air, as a live television demonstration.

physics-001.question: what really decides it
physics-001.line: Air push grows as you fall faster, until it matches the pull of gravity. Then you stop speeding up and fall at a steady speed.

physics-001.question: where it is used
physics-001.line: Parachutes work because a large area gives a lot of air push, so the falling speed levels off at a much lower value.

chem-001.question: what and where
chem-001.line: Baking soda and vinegar react and make new substances. One of them is carbon dioxide gas, and the bubbles you see are that gas escaping.

chem-001.question: how
chem-001.line: The gas escapes into the air.

chem-001.question: how
chem-001.line: In a sealed system the mass stays the same.

chem-001.question: why
chem-001.line: The reaction keeps producing carbon dioxide gas in a fixed space.

chem-001.question: what if
chem-001.line: In a sealed tube the pressure can pop the lid off, so eye protection is advised.

chem-001.question: where it is used
chem-001.line: Baking: sodium hydrogencarbonate with an acid releases carbon dioxide that makes mixtures rise.
